`pitw` compares a set of continuous predictive distributions with the values
they were meant to predict. For example, given forecasts of a hospital admission
rate and the corresponding observed rates, we can check whether the predictive
distributions tend to be too narrow or too wide after accounting for a common
location bias.

For each observation, the probability integral transform (PIT) gives the
proportion of its predictive distribution below the observed value. For
calibrated continuous predictions these proportions should be uniform between
zero and one. The package summarises departures from uniformity in three ways.

| Score | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| `B_pit` | Overall departure from uniformity in the original PIT values. Bias, spread and distribution shape can all contribute. |
| `U_pit` | Departure that remains after estimating and adjusting for one common location shift. |
| `D_pit` | Direction of the remaining spread discrepancy. Positive values indicate overconfidence and negative values indicate underconfidence. |

## Score a set of forecasts

We use 100 reference quantiles of a standard normal distribution as example
observations. Each forecast is normal with mean 0.5 and standard deviation 0.7,
so the forecasts are displaced and too narrow by construction.

```{r score-forecasts}
observed <- stats::qnorm(stats::ppoints(100))

pitw::pit_w(true_value = observed, location = 0.5, scale = 0.7)
```

The positive `D_pit` shows that the forecasts are too narrow after adjustment
for the common shift. This example illustrates the scores. The significance
tests use large-sample reference distributions and assume independent
predictions, which matters when forecasts or estimates use overlapping data.

`pit_w()` scores one set of predictions. Use `prediction_scores()` to score
several sets in a grouped data frame and compare the PIT scores with coverage,
interval width and the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS).

## Read the vignettes in order

1. [PIT histograms and forecast calibration](introduction-to-pit.html). Use
   simulated forecasts to see how location bias and predictive spread change
   the histogram.
2. [The three PIT-Wasserstein scores](pit-w-metrics.html). See how the scores
   are calculated and how they behave alongside coverage and CRPS.
3. [Scoring reproduction number estimates from EpiEstim](sir-epiestim-example.html).
   Compare estimates with known $R_t$ across simulated epidemics of different
   sizes.
4. [Significance testing](significance-testing.html). See how to use the
   reference distributions and which assumptions matter for interpretation.
5. [Sample size and power](sample-sizes-and-power.html). Compare how the scores
   separate known differences as the number of predictions increases.
6. [Predictive distribution shape](model-misspecification.html). See what
   happens when forecasts use a different distributional family, including
   cases where width and tail differences produce similar scores.
